question: European register of looted cultural goods

On 3 September 2026, the Register of Damage for Ukraine launched categories B2 and C2 for the registration of claims in respect of the damage, destruction or loss of objects and buildings of cultural value.

The mechanism covers museums, archives, libraries, religious buildings, works of art, archaeological finds and collections, as well as the costs of the search for, recovery, restitution, conservation and protection of heritage. The Council of Europe recognises that damage encompasses not only the value of the destroyed or looted object, but also the costs of its identification and recovery.

The mechanism concerns the Russian aggression of 24 February 2022 and sets a new standard which should be applied to victims of looting during World War II – including Poland, whose works of art remain abroad, mainly in Germany. Given that the EU is party to/a participant in the register for which categories B2 and C2 were launched on 3 September 2026: 1.
Does the Commission also recognise the costs of the search for and restitution of Ukrainian cultural goods as compensable damage?
Does the Commission take the view that the costs of the search for, identification and restitution of cultural goods looted by Germany in World War II similarly form part of the compensable damage?

Will it consider setting up a European register of looted cultural goods, encompassing the value of objects looted by Germany during World War II, as well as legal expenses and the costs of identification and restitution?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.11.2026) The EU has condemned the looting, destruction and illicit trafficking of Ukrainian cultural goods in the context of Russia’s war of aggression.

The EU has consistently supported efforts to protect Ukraine’s cultural heritage and facilitate the return of goods, for example, via the International Council of Museums for the project on Prevention, Research, Investigation and Security in Museums.

The EU is a Participant to the Register of Damage for Ukraine, under which eligible claims may include expenses related to the search, recovery, return and restitution of lost cultural values, including costs incurred for securing their return.

The existence of these categories does not establish an EU legal regime governing historical restitution claims or determine the compensability of categories of expenditure in such cases. The Commission regards the safeguarding of all forms of cultural heritage with the utmost importance, in line with Article 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

The principle that States must make reparation for internationally wrongful acts is part of customary international law and is reflected in the Draft Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts.

Under Article 3(5) and Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union, the EU is bound by customary international law in its external action, however, at present the EU lacks competence to enforce this principle between, or on behalf of its Member States.
